stem: What is a sexually transmitted infection (STI)?

options.content: An infection caused only by bacteria
options.rationale: STIs can be caused by bacteria or viruses.

options.content: An infection that is transmitted through sexual contact
options.rationale: For example HIV, gonorrhoea and syphilis.

options.content: An infection that is inherited from the parents
options.rationale: Infections are caused by pathogens, not inherited.

options.content: Any infection of the reproductive organs, however it is caught
options.rationale: STIs are defined by how they are transmitted.

explanation: A sexually transmitted infection is an infection that is transmitted through sexual contact, such as HIV, gonorrhoea or syphilis.

stem: What type of pathogen is HIV?

options.content: A bacterium
options.rationale: HIV is not a bacterium, so antibiotics do not affect it.

options.content: A fungus
options.rationale: HIV is not a fungus.

options.content: A virus
options.rationale: HIV is the human immunodeficiency virus.

options.content: A protoctist
options.rationale: Protoctists cause diseases such as malaria.

explanation: HIV, the human immunodeficiency virus, is a virus. It infects and destroys lymphocytes and may lead to AIDS.

stem: Name the condition, in which the immune system is very weak, that untreated HIV infection may lead to.

rejected.feedback: HIV is the virus. The late stage of untreated infection is AIDS.
TB is one of the infections that can affect people with AIDS.
Tuberculosis is an opportunistic infection, not the condition itself.

explanation: Untreated HIV infection may lead to AIDS (acquired immune deficiency syndrome), when the immune system is so weak that serious opportunistic infections develop.

stem: True or false: HIV can be passed on by mosquito bites.

answerSpec.feedbackTrue: Not so. HIV cannot multiply in mosquitoes, and a mosquito injects saliva, not blood from the last person it bit.
answerSpec.feedbackFalse: Correct. Mosquitoes do not transmit HIV.

explanation: HIV cannot survive and multiply inside mosquitoes, and mosquitoes inject saliva, not blood, when they bite. HIV is passed on through sex, infected blood and from mother to baby.

stem: Which of these can transmit HIV?

options.content: Shaking hands with a person who has HIV
options.rationale: HIV is not passed on by touch.

options.content: Sharing a needle with a person who has HIV
options.rationale: Infected blood can be injected into the next user.

options.content: Sharing a plate of food with a person who has HIV
options.rationale: HIV is not passed on in food or on plates.

options.content: Using the same toilet as a person who has HIV
options.rationale: HIV is not passed on this way.

explanation: HIV is passed on through unprotected sex, through infected blood (for example on shared needles) and from mother to baby. It is not passed on by touch, food, plates or toilets.

stem: Select **all** the ways in which HIV is **not** transmitted.

options.content: Hugging
options.rationale: Touch does not transmit HIV.

options.content: Unprotected sexual intercourse
options.rationale: This is the main route of transmission.

options.content: Sharing cups
options.rationale: HIV is not passed on in saliva on cups.

options.content: Breastfeeding by a mother with untreated HIV
options.rationale: HIV can pass to a baby in breast milk.

options.content: Mosquito bites
options.rationale: Mosquitoes do not transmit HIV.

options.content: Sharing needles for injecting drugs
options.rationale: Infected blood can be passed on.

options.content: Swimming in the same pool
options.rationale: Water does not transmit HIV.

explanation: HIV is passed on only through sexual fluids, blood and from mother to baby (pregnancy, birth, breastfeeding). It is not passed on by hugging, sharing cups, mosquito bites or swimming together.
hints: HIV is passed on in body fluids such as semen, vaginal fluids, blood and breast milk.

stem: How does antiretroviral therapy (ART) help a person living with HIV?

options.content: It kills all the HIV in the body, so the infection is cured
options.rationale: ART controls HIV but does not cure it.

options.content: It vaccinates the person so that they never develop AIDS
options.rationale: ART is a treatment, not a vaccine.

options.content: It is an antibiotic that kills the bacteria that cause HIV
options.rationale: HIV is a virus; antibiotics do not affect it.

options.content: It keeps the virus in the blood very low, so the immune system recovers
options.rationale: The person can stay healthy and is much less likely to pass HIV on.

explanation: ART stops HIV multiplying, keeping the amount of virus in the blood very low. The lymphocyte count recovers, so the person stays healthy; when the virus is undetectable, HIV is not passed on through sex. ART must be taken every day because it is not a cure.

stem: How do condoms reduce the spread of STIs?

options.content: They are a barrier, so body fluids do not pass between partners
options.rationale: Pathogens in semen and vaginal fluids are kept apart.

options.content: They contain antibiotics that kill the pathogens in semen
options.rationale: Condoms do not contain antibiotics.

options.content: They stop ovulation, so no infected egg can be released
options.rationale: Condoms do not affect ovulation.

options.content: They release chemicals that make the immune system stronger
options.rationale: Condoms do not affect the immune system.

explanation: A condom is a barrier: it stops semen, vaginal fluids and blood passing between partners, so the pathogens they may carry are not transmitted. It must be used correctly every time.
hints: What does a condom stop from passing between partners?

stem: What is the purpose of contact tracing in the control of STIs?

options.content: To find the mosquitoes that carried the infection to the person
options.rationale: STIs are not carried by mosquitoes.

options.content: To find, test and treat the sexual partners of an infected person
options.rationale: This stops further spread and reinfection.

options.content: To make a list of infected people who must stay at home
options.rationale: Contact tracing is not about keeping people at home.

options.content: To trace the source of the contaminated water the person drank
options.rationale: That is used for waterborne diseases such as cholera.

explanation: Contact tracing finds and informs the sexual partners of a person with an STI, so they can be tested and treated. This prevents complications, stops further spread and stops the treated person being re-infected.

stem: Match each sexually transmitted infection with its pathogen and main sign.

right.content: Bacterium; burning pain when urinating and a discharge
Bacterium; a painless sore, later a rash on the palms and soles
Bacterium; painful soft sores and swollen glands in the groin
Virus; painful blisters that keep coming back
Virus; small lumps on or around the genitals

explanation: Gonorrhoea, syphilis and chancroid are bacterial; genital herpes and genital warts are viral. A protoctist causing fever every few days describes malaria, which is not an STI.
hints: Which of the STIs are caused by viruses?

stem: Select **all** the STIs that can be cured with antibiotics.

options.content: Gonorrhoea
options.rationale: It is caused by a bacterium.

options.content: HIV
options.rationale: HIV is a virus; ART controls it but does not cure it.

options.content: Syphilis
options.rationale: It is caused by a bacterium and is treated with penicillin.

options.content: Genital herpes
options.rationale: It is caused by a virus and cannot be cured.

options.content: Chancroid
options.rationale: It is caused by a bacterium.

options.content: Genital warts
options.rationale: They are caused by a virus.

explanation: Antibiotics cure bacterial STIs: gonorrhoea, syphilis and chancroid. Viral STIs (HIV, genital herpes, genital warts) cannot be cured by antibiotics.

stem: Untreated gonorrhoea can make a woman infertile. How?

options.content: The bacteria destroy all the eggs stored in the ovaries
options.rationale: The main problem is in the oviducts.

options.content: The bacteria turn into a virus that attacks the uterus lining
options.rationale: Bacteria cannot turn into viruses.

options.content: The bacteria make a hormone that stops the menstrual cycle
options.rationale: Gonorrhoea does not work by producing hormones.

options.content: Scarring of the oviducts blocks the passage of eggs and sperm
options.rationale: Sperm and egg cannot meet.

explanation: Untreated gonorrhoea can spread to the oviducts, causing inflammation and scarring. Blocked oviducts stop sperm meeting the egg, so the woman may become infertile. Early treatment with antibiotics prevents this.
hints: Where do sperm and egg normally meet?

stem: Why are people with untreated HIV more likely to suffer from tuberculosis and pneumonia?

options.content: HIV changes into the bacteria that cause these diseases
options.rationale: Viruses do not change into bacteria.

options.content: HIV makes the lungs produce more mucus
options.rationale: This is not how HIV causes these infections.

options.content: HIV destroys lymphocytes, so the body cannot fight other pathogens
options.rationale: These are opportunistic infections.

options.content: People with HIV are given antibiotics, which cause these diseases
options.rationale: Antibiotics do not cause TB or pneumonia.

explanation: HIV destroys lymphocytes. With fewer lymphocytes, fewer antibodies are made, so pathogens that a healthy immune system would control cause opportunistic infections such as TB and pneumonia.

stem: Why is regular testing important for controlling the spread of STIs, including HIV?

options.content: Testing cures the infection, so the person cannot pass it on
options.rationale: A test only shows whether a person is infected.

options.content: Testing makes a person immune, so they cannot catch STIs again
options.rationale: Tests do not give immunity.

options.content: STIs always cause obvious symptoms, so testing confirms what people know
options.rationale: Many STIs have no obvious symptoms.

options.content: Many infected people have no symptoms, so they may pass it on unknowingly
options.rationale: Testing lets them get treatment and protect partners.

explanation: Many people with STIs, including HIV and gonorrhoea in women, have no symptoms. Testing finds the infection, so the person can be treated and can protect their partners.
hints: Can you always tell that someone has an STI?

stem: At her first antenatal visit, a pregnant woman is tested for syphilis and the test is positive. She had noticed a painless sore some months ago, but it had healed by itself.

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: What type of pathogen causes syphilis?

options.content: A bacterium
options.rationale: Syphilis is bacterial.

options.content: A virus
options.rationale: Syphilis is not caused by a virus.

options.content: A protoctist
options.rationale: Protoctists cause diseases such as malaria.

options.content: A fungus
options.rationale: Syphilis is not a fungal infection.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Explain why it is important to test pregnant women for syphilis.

points.description: Syphilis can cross the placenta / be passed to the baby
It can cause stillbirth or a baby born with syphilis (congenital syphilis); early treatment protects the baby

parts.explanation: Syphilis bacteria can cross the placenta, causing stillbirth or a baby born with syphilis; treating the mother early protects the baby.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: Name the type of medicine used to treat syphilis.

rejected.feedback: ARVs control HIV; syphilis is treated with antibiotics.
Syphilis is bacterial, so it is treated with antibiotics.
Painkillers do not kill the bacteria.

parts.label: (d)
parts.stem: Explain why her sexual partner should also be tested and treated.

points.description: He may also be infected (and may not know / have no symptoms)
If he is not treated he could re-infect her after her treatment, and could pass the infection to others (contact tracing)

parts.explanation: He may be infected without knowing it; if he is not treated he could re-infect her after treatment and infect others.

parts.label: (e)
parts.stem: If syphilis is not treated, what can happen many years later?

options.content: It always clears up completely by itself
options.rationale: Without treatment, syphilis can progress to later stages.

options.content: The heart, brain and nerves can be damaged
options.rationale: This happens in the late stage of untreated syphilis.

options.content: It turns into HIV
options.rationale: A bacterial infection cannot turn into a virus.

options.content: The person becomes immune to all STIs
options.rationale: Syphilis does not give immunity to other STIs.

explanation: Syphilis is bacterial and can cross the placenta, so pregnant women are tested. It is cured with antibiotics such as penicillin, and partners must be treated too. Untreated, it can damage the heart, brain and nerves years later.
workedSolution:
**(a)** A bacterium.

**(b)** It can cross the placenta, causing stillbirth or congenital syphilis.

**(c)** Antibiotics, such as penicillin.

**(d)** He may be infected; he could re-infect her or infect others.

**(e)** Damage to the heart, brain and nerves.
hints: Can syphilis bacteria cross the placenta?

stem: This question is about HIV.

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: Which cells does HIV infect and destroy?

options.content: Red blood cells, which carry oxygen
options.rationale: HIV does not destroy red blood cells.

options.content: Nerve cells in the spinal cord
options.rationale: These are not the main target of HIV.

options.content: A type of lymphocyte (white blood cell)
options.rationale: This weakens the immune system.

options.content: Cells in the outer layer of the skin
options.rationale: Skin cells are not HIV's target.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Describe **three** ways in which the spread of HIV can be reduced.

points.description: One method with how it works, e.g. abstinence / being faithful to one tested partner
A second method, e.g. using condoms correctly every time (barrier to body fluids); not sharing needles; screening donated blood
A third method, e.g. testing and antiretroviral therapy (reduces the virus in the blood); PMTCT; PrEP; medical male circumcision (partial protection)

parts.explanation: For example: using condoms every time, which stop body fluids being exchanged; never sharing needles; and HIV testing with antiretroviral treatment, which keeps the virus in the blood very low.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: Name the type of treatment taken every day by people living with HIV to keep the virus under control.

rejected.feedback: There is no vaccine against HIV; it is controlled with antiretroviral therapy.
Penicillin is an antibiotic and does not affect HIV.

explanation: HIV destroys lymphocytes. Its spread is reduced by abstinence, faithfulness, condoms, not sharing needles, screening blood, testing, ART, PMTCT and PrEP. Antiretroviral therapy controls the virus but does not cure it.
workedSolution:
**(a)** A type of lymphocyte.

**(b)** For example, condoms, not sharing needles, testing and ART.

**(c)** Antiretroviral therapy (ARVs).
hints: Think about sex, blood and mother-to-baby routes.

stem: Explain how the spread of sexually transmitted infections, including HIV, can be controlled. [6]

points.description: Abstinence: no sexual contact, so no sexual transmission
Faithfulness to one partner whose status is known / fewer sexual partners reduces the chance of meeting an infected partner
Condoms used correctly every time act as a barrier to body fluids
Testing, so infected people know their status and get treatment
Treatment: antibiotics cure bacterial STIs; ART lowers the amount of HIV, so it is less likely (or not) passed on
Contact tracing: partners are found, tested and treated, preventing reinfection and further spread
Preventing transmission through blood and to babies: screening blood, not sharing needles, PMTCT
Education about how STIs are and are not spread, reducing stigma so people seek testing

answerSpec.modelAnswer: **Abstinence** prevents sexual transmission completely, and being **faithful** to one partner whose HIV status is known, or having **fewer partners**, reduces the chance of meeting an infected person. **Condoms**, used correctly every time, form a **barrier** so that body fluids are not exchanged. **Testing** lets infected people know their status: bacterial STIs can then be **cured with antibiotics**, and HIV can be controlled with **antiretroviral therapy**, which keeps the virus so low that it is not passed on through sex. **Contact tracing** finds and treats partners, stopping reinfection and further spread. Transmission through blood is prevented by **screening donated blood** and not sharing needles, and **PMTCT** protects babies. Education helps people understand how STIs are spread and reduces stigma, so more people come forward for testing.

explanation: Each mark needs a measure and how it reduces transmission.
hints: Think about sexual behaviour, barriers, testing and treatment, and the blood and mother-to-baby routes.

stem: Compare bacterial and viral sexually transmitted infections. Give examples of each and explain how they are treated. [5]

points.description: Examples of bacterial STIs: gonorrhoea, syphilis, chancroid
Examples of viral STIs: HIV, genital herpes, genital warts
Bacterial STIs can be cured with antibiotics (e.g. penicillin for syphilis)
Viral STIs cannot be cured with antibiotics (antibiotics do not affect viruses)
Viral STIs can be controlled: ART for HIV, antiviral medicine for herpes, removal of warts; the virus may remain
Both kinds are spread by sexual contact and prevented by abstinence, faithfulness and condoms

answerSpec.modelAnswer: **Bacterial STIs** include **gonorrhoea, syphilis and chancroid**. They can be **cured with antibiotics**, for example penicillin for syphilis, especially if treated early. **Viral STIs** include **HIV, genital herpes and genital warts**. Antibiotics have no effect on viruses, so these infections **cannot be cured**, but they can be **controlled**: antiretroviral therapy keeps HIV under control, antiviral medicine reduces outbreaks of herpes, and warts can be removed, although the virus may remain. Both kinds are spread by sexual contact and are prevented in the same ways: abstinence, faithfulness and condoms.

explanation: Give examples of each type and contrast the treatment: curable with antibiotics, or controllable but not curable.
hints: Which STIs are bacterial, and which are viral?

stem: True or false: genital herpes can be cured with a course of antibiotics.

answerSpec.feedbackTrue: Not so. Genital herpes is caused by a virus, so antibiotics have no effect; antiviral medicine can reduce outbreaks.
answerSpec.feedbackFalse: Correct. Herpes is viral: it cannot be cured, although antiviral medicine reduces outbreaks.

explanation: Genital herpes is caused by the herpes simplex virus. Antibiotics do not affect viruses, so there is no cure; antiviral medicines reduce how often painful blisters return.
hints: Is herpes caused by a bacterium or a virus?

stem: What does a prevention of mother-to-child transmission (PMTCT) programme aim to do?

options.content: To cure mothers of HIV before their babies are born
options.rationale: There is no cure for HIV.

options.content: To stop all mothers with HIV from ever breastfeeding
options.rationale: Feeding advice is given, but this is not the aim.

options.content: To reduce the chance of HIV passing from a mother to her baby
options.rationale: ART and preventive medicine protect the baby.

options.content: To vaccinate newborn babies so that they never catch HIV
options.rationale: There is no HIV vaccine.

explanation: PMTCT programmes test pregnant women for HIV and give ART to mothers who have it and preventive medicine to their babies, greatly reducing the chance of the baby being infected.

stem: A man was infected with HIV two years ago. He feels completely well, has not been tested and is not on treatment. Which statement is correct?

options.content: He cannot have HIV, because people with HIV always have symptoms
options.rationale: People with HIV can feel well for years.

options.content: He has AIDS, because everyone with HIV has AIDS from the start
options.rationale: AIDS is the late stage of untreated infection.

options.content: He cannot pass the virus on until he develops AIDS and becomes ill
options.rationale: HIV can be passed on at any stage without treatment.

options.content: He has HIV, may not have AIDS yet, and can pass the virus on
options.rationale: Testing and treatment would protect him and his partners.

explanation: A person can live with untreated HIV for years without symptoms, before AIDS develops, but can pass the virus on throughout. Testing and starting ART would protect both his health and his partners.
hints: Is HIV the same as AIDS?
